I work in public safety telecommunications (9-1-1 here in the US). There is a law referred to as the Kelsey Smith Act that allows public safety agencies to obtain subscriber information, to include billing address and GPS tracking information, without the subscriber's prior consent and without a warrant or a court order. To do so, we have to be able to demonstrate that there is a reasonable likelihood that the subscriber is in immediate physical danger, and that the subscriber would reasonably contact 9-1-1 if they were able. I can attest from personal experience that information obtained this way definitely saves lives. That exemption for instances of immediate danger of death would allow us to continue this practice.

That said, even Kelsey Smith constitutes a violation of 4th amendment protections against illegal seizure of private personal information. On the local level at least, cell service providers routinely deny requests that do not meet the standard for a Kelsey Smith request (they don't want to get sued). And I can't tell you how often the police ask us to obtain cell phone information without meeting either of the above-mentioned criteria. I spent ten minutes explaining to a homicide detective why we couldn't track the cell phone of someone suspected of murder, even citing the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals decision from August 5th (article, ruling).

This has little to do with the federal government spying, of course. Just adding a smaller-scale perspective to this colossal overreach on the part of the state. It is very difficult for local law enforcement to this kind of information (unless you're a huge department like the NYPD, perhaps).
